source.title: To grok or not to grok: Disentangling generalization and memorization on corrupted algorithmic datasets
source.authors: Darshil Doshi; Aritra Das; Tian-Yu He; Andrey Gromov

record.tranche_reason: The study tests grokking and related mechanisms on modular arithmetic, but focuses on corrupted labels, MLPs, IPR, and pruning rather than reproducing the original setup alone.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on modular-arithmetic grokking, IPR dynamics, neuron pruning, and regularization. Its MNIST experiment reports final phase outcomes but not delayed generalization dynamics, so it is not recorded as a result for V3. Numerical values visible only in plots are not inferred.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces grokking on clean modular addition: test accuracy shows a sharp transition long after overfitting (Fig. 2), and IPR tracks periodic weights. It extends this to a new setting, corrupted labels with regularization, reporting how weight decay moves generalization boundaries and suppresses memorizing neurons. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one fix: BatchNorm de-amplifies memorizing neurons. Missing is the authors' dynamics claim: with regularization, training first groks, then unlearns memorized corrupted labels, so train accuracy drops to about 100(1−ξ)%.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses modular arithmetic with deliberately corrupted training labels, primarily quadratic-activation MLPs, and examines IPR, pruning, weight decay, dropout, and BatchNorm. Its default optimizer and loss are AdamW and MSE.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcomes vary with data fraction, corruption fraction, and regularization strength. The paper also reports differences by architecture, activation, loss, batch size, and optimizer in its appendices.

fits_no_version.finding: In trained networks, separable generalizing (high-IPR) and memorizing (low-IPR) sub-networks coexist. Pruning one set selectively removes test or corrupted-label accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalizing and memorizing circuits in grokked networks are distinct, separable sub-networks identifiable by a periodicity measure.

fits_no_version.finding: Dropout shifts IPR toward generalizing neurons. BatchNorm instead de-amplifies memorizing neurons without eliminating them.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularizers other than low-norm biases favour the generalizing circuit through distinct mechanisms.

fits_no_version.finding: Under very high weight decay with Adam and quadratic activation, grokked networks later collapse to chance as weight norms vanish.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokked solutions can be lost under excessive weight decay with adaptive optimizers (Forgetting).

record.problems: Most reported phase-diagram and pruning outcomes are qualitative descriptions of plots rather than numerical values in text. The paper does not compare clean-data grokking delay across training-set sizes. The default phase diagrams are empirical, and the text does not give uncertainty for most reported conditions.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. The MNIST result is not included because it reports final regularization outcomes but not delayed-grokking dynamics relevant to the listed versions.

untested.parts: Whether the grokking delay grows as the training set shrinks. No clean-label delay-versus-data-fraction comparison is reported.
Whether IPR quantitatively anticipates the test-accuracy jump; the text says only that it rises monotonically. Removal of memorizing components on clean data.
Delayed generalization on non-algorithmic data. The MNIST result reports endpoint phases only. A lazy-to-rich switch of the delay is not tested; Appendix G.3 reports IPR shifts only.
The efficiency account itself, any explicit critical dataset size, and ungrokking below it.
Whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm. The universality of periodic embeddings (Hypothesis 2.2) is asserted from IPR histograms only.

missing.what: Two-stage dynamics under regularization: the network first groks, then unlearns memorized corrupted labels. Train accuracy drops from about 100% to 100(1−ξ)%.
Weight decay promotes generalization over memorization in 1-layer Transformers and 3-layer ReLU MLPs, and is essential there for Full Inversion.
The weight-decay pattern holds across settings, but regularization needs differ: ReLU and CrossEntropy need more regularization, and modular multiplication gives near-identical phase diagrams.
Periodic (high-IPR) embeddings appear across Transformer configurations; head count and weight tying shift the IPR distribution.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 limits_scope (R11) and V5 limits_scope (R12) are dropped: R11 is a fixed-budget endpoint, and R12 is a different phenomenon (Forgetting). The V2 support from the pruning rows (R5–R8) is moved to fits_no_version, because pruning shows separable circuits, not their timing. Phase labels come from final accuracies after 2000 steps; most results are qualitative descriptions of plots.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not compare grokking delay across training-set sizes in the clean-label setting.

It does not establish that memorizing components are naturally removed later in training; pruning is an intervention, and the reported IPR trend does not establish that it anticipates the accuracy transition.
The MNIST experiment does not report grokking-like delayed generalization or test whether initialization scale or a lazy-to-rich transition switches it on or off.
No LLM pretraining or realistic large-model fine-tuning is studied.
The study does not test an efficiency account, identify a critical dataset size, or show ungrokking below such a size.
The study does not compare whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
The study does not test whether grokking is an adaptive-optimizer or floating-point artifact that disappears when controlled.

rows.operation_detail: Compare per-neuron IPR distributions across regularization strengths.
rows.baseline: The no-regularization Coexistence phase has a bimodal IPR distribution.
rows.value: With weight decay, the distribution shifts toward higher IPR; in Full Inversion, memorizing neurons are almost entirely eliminated in favour of generalizing ones.

rows.subject: 2-layer MLP with quadratic activation
rows.operation_detail: Compare per-neuron IPR distributions across dropout strengths.
rows.baseline: The no-regularization Coexistence phase has a bimodal IPR distribution.
rows.value: With dropout, the distribution shifts toward higher IPR; in Full Inversion, memorizing neurons are almost entirely eliminated in favour of generalizing ones.
rows.check: Dropout is not a low-norm bias. The paper attributes its effect to redundancy of periodic neurons, not efficiency. It is an endpoint comparison, so it does not show V2 dynamics either. Recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: 2-layer MLP with quadratic activation
rows.operation_detail: Progressively prune neurons starting with the lowest-IPR neurons from a trained network.
rows.baseline: Before pruning, the network has near-100% accuracy on train and test data.
rows.value: Accuracy on corrupted examples decreases monotonically as more low-IPR neurons are pruned.
rows.note: The paper states that accuracy on corrupted examples falls as low-IPR neurons are removed.
rows.check: Post-training pruning shows that separable memorizing and generalizing sub-networks coexist. It says nothing about when either forms or is removed, so it does not measure what V2 names.

rows.subject: 2-layer MLP with quadratic activation
rows.operation_detail: Train with weight decay and measure generalization and memorization on corrupted modular addition.
rows.baseline: With no regularization, the described Coexistence phase has both train and test accuracy close to 100%.
rows.value: In Full Inversion, test accuracy is 100% while training accuracy plateaus close to 100(1 − ξ)%; the network does not memorize corrupted examples.
rows.note: This supports a weight-decay effect on generalization versus memorization; it does not establish an efficiency account.

rows.measure: Training and test accuracy in the Memorization phase
rows.baseline: Random guessing accuracy on test data
rows.value: Training accuracy is close to 100%, while test accuracy is at random-guessing level.
rows.note: This is an endpoint phase description; the text does not say whether test accuracy later rises in these conditions.
rows.check: Phases are classified at the end of a fixed 2000-step budget. A Memorization endpoint cannot show whether grokking would occur later, so it is not 'absent' for V1. The condition also mixes low data fraction with high label corruption.

rows.subject: 2-layer MLP with quadratic activation
rows.operation_detail: Train with very high weight decay and track accuracy and weight norms.

conditions.value: adaptive optimizer; Adam in the appendix account

rows.measure: Training and test accuracy, and weight norms over training
rows.baseline: The network initially reaches the Full Inversion pattern: high test accuracy and training accuracy near 100(1 − ξ)%.
rows.value: Both accuracies subsequently fall to random-guessing levels as weight norms decay to arbitrarily small values.
rows.note: The authors state that this forgetting occurs with adaptive optimizers and activation functions whose first nonzero series term has degree at least 2.
rows.check: Forgetting means collapse after grokking under extreme weight decay (20) with adaptive optimizers. V5's ungrokking is a drop below a critical dataset size, not this. No version names this effect. Recorded under fits_no_version.

source_check.notes:
R3 compares trained endpoints across regularization strengths; it is not a measurement of temporal neuron removal. Very high decay produces subsequent forgetting (Appendix E), so the beneficial decay trend is not unlimited.
V2's predictive lead time and V5's circuit-efficiency explanation, critical-size prediction and ungrokking remain untested.
